Neonatal Spinetail mobula pups are born at a total length of approximately 100 cm [Lb = approximately 100 cm], immediately entering a pelagic existence after emerging from the maternal oviduct. Available records indicate that the disc width at birth typically ranges between 85 and 92 cm [Lb = between 85 and 92 cm], a dimension that reflects the considerable size of the offspring relative to the adult female. This large birth size is characteristic of many mobulid rays, where a single, well-developed pup is produced per gestation event, thereby enhancing early survival in the oligotrophic waters these animals frequent. The developing embryo relies entirely on a yolk-dependent phase within the uterus before transitioning to free-swimming existence. Field observations suggest that the period of in utero development is governed by a gestation interval of approximately one year, after which parturition of the solitary neonate occurs.

At the onset of maturity, female Spinetail mobula attain a disc width at puberty of approximately 218 cm [Lp = approximately 218 cm], a threshold that signals the commencement of ovarian maturation and reproductive capability. Growth toward this size is gradual, with individuals investing considerable somatic energy into reaching the body dimensions necessary for successful gestation. Comparative studies with other mobulid species indicate that this pubertal size represents a substantial proportion of the ultimate disc width, which for females can reach or exceed 310 cm [Li = 310 cm]. Some sources report that exceptionally large females may attain a disc width of up to 9 m [Li = 9 m], though such extreme values likely reflect the upper bounds of individual variation encountered in oceanic populations. The attainment of this ultimate size is thought to require several years of sustained feeding in productive oceanic zones.

The reproductive output of the Spinetail mobula is characterized by a remarkably low maximum reproductive rate, constrained by a lengthy gestation period and an extended interval between successive breeding events. Under the oceanic thermal conditions typical of its tropical and subtropical habitat, approximately 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], females produce a single pup per gestation event [N_R_i = single pup per gestation event]. The interval between successive pregnancies corresponds to approximately one pregnancy every 2 to 5 years [F_R_i = approximately one pregnancy every 2 to 5 years], a protracted cycle that reflects the considerable energetic expenditure associated with producing a large, well-developed offspring. This low reproductive frequency aligns with the species' slow life-history strategy.

Embryonic development proceeds entirely within the maternal reproductive tract, with the age at birth measured from the moment of internal fertilisation. At the ambient water temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], the gestation period extends for approximately 365 days [ab = approximately 365 days], culminating in the parturition of a single free-swimming pup. This year-long developmental window allows for the full differentiation of the wing-like pectoral fins and the characteristic elongate tail spine that defines the species. The precise timing of parturition may be influenced by local oceanographic conditions, though the thermal regime of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C] appears to represent a consistent baseline for the completion of embryogenesis across the species' range.

Longevity data from mark-recapture studies and age-determination analyses of vertebral centra suggest that the Spinetail mobula exhibits a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years], when assessed under the thermal conditions of its typical habitat at 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C]. Some estimates extend this range to between 15 and 20 years [am = between 15 and 20 years], depending on local environmental stressors and predation pressure at a temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C]. Age-related senescence in this species manifests as reduced fecundity and diminished foraging efficiency in the oldest individuals, eventually leading to natural mortality. The moderate longevity relative to its body size is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritises high investment in each offspring over rapid population turnover. This suite of life-history traits renders the Spinetail mobula particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic threats such as fisheries bycatch.
